en: One who meditates on the heart-mantra wheel of Tārā shall remain unstained by the defects of death;
devoted to this practice for a period of six months, one will attain all siddhis. (Mṛtyuvañcanasitatārāsādhana 1)
Extracted from the *Mṛtyuvañcana-saṃgraha* (The Compendium on Deceiving Death) by the command of Vāgīśvara,
this meditation on Sitatārā destroys all fear.
In the sky shimmering with the formless radiance of the first of the four groups [of syllables],
having beheld the white lotus and moon seat before him, one should recite the threefold refuge.
For a moment, one should contemplate emptiness in order to abandon the superimpositions of ordinary beings;
thereafter, through the power of one's aspiration, the syllable of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) shall arise.
Seated upon a moon-disc throne situated in the center of a white lotus,
she sits with her legs bound in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, holding a gesture of granting boons and an utpala lotus.
Having the form of the autumn moon’s rays, seated upon a moon at her back,
fully adorned with all ornaments, and possessing the body of a sixteen-year-old.

Having meditated upon Noble Tārā, the mother of all the perfectly awakened Buddhas and their sons, who can assume any form at will, within one's heart, one should visualize her wheel as having white radiance.
The eight-square grid is filled with eight syllables;
the name of the one to be accomplished, preceded by *oṃ* and *hā*, is situated in the center of the consonants at the navel.
With a one-pointed mind and firm resolve, one should meditate for six months;
with an undaunted heart, one should recite this ten-syllable mantra. (Mvsts 9)
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, one should subsequently employ Tāre;
then Tuttāre, followed by Ture, ending with Svāhā—this is the mantra for all rites.
Even by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, the Moon, the Sun, Rudra, the world-protectors, and Manmatha,
he whose hair-tips remain unbroken conquers death like one who is liberated.
It brings about the destruction of wrinkles, graying hair, misfortune, disease, and poverty;
it is the eradicator of the mass of suffering caused by the eight great fears, such as lions and the like.
The acquisition of garments, drinks, palaces, jewels, and so forth without asking;
and the supernatural attainments such as the sword, collyrium, foot-ointment, and the auspicious jar.
Poetic skill, eloquence, intelligence, and utterly pure wisdom, as well as other desired accomplishments, arise from this wheel. (Mvsts 14)
By whatever merit is gained from extracting this sadhana of Sitatārā, which destroys death and disease,
may the world itself become Tārā.
The Sadhana of Sitatārā for Deceiving Death.
